pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7. Mentally find 10 more or 10 less than a two-digit number WITHOUT counting on in ones — 10 more than 56 is 66, 10 less is 46 — by recognising that adding/subtracting a ten changes only the tens digit (the ones stay put).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 1/2): 'given a number, identify one more and one less'; Year 2 place-value and mental strategies building toward 'add and subtract … a two-digit number and tens'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.5 'given a two-digit number, mentally find 10 more or 10 less than the number, without having to count; explain the reasoning used'; extended by 2.NBT.8.
• Operational details — Use the 100-square (move straight DOWN a row for +10, UP for -10) and base-ten rods (add/remove one rod) so the child SEES the ones column untouched and only the tens change. Move quickly from concrete to the mental generalisation and demand the explanation ('the ones stay the same, the tens go up by one'). Watch the decade boundary and the ones-digit-unchanged rule.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6, emerging): finds 10 more/less using a 100-square, moving a row. Tier B (age 6-7, secure): states 10 more/less of any two-digit number mentally and explains the tens digit changes. Tier C (age 7, extending): does it fluently across decade boundaries and justifies why the ones digit never changes.
bestPractices: Exploit the 100-square structure: +10 is one row DOWN, -10 is one row UP, in the same column — the visual makes 'ones unchanged, tens ±1' obvious.
Use tens-rods: add or remove exactly ONE rod and narrate that the cubes (ones) never moved.
Insist on the generalised explanation, not just the answer, so it becomes reasoning rather than counting.
Contrast with '1 more/1 less' so the child distinguishes changing the ones from changing the tens.
Rehearse across decade boundaries to build fluency and flag where the pattern needs care.
keyRepresentations: Base-ten tens-rods and ones-cubes (add/remove one rod)
Place-value chart showing only the tens digit changing
Gattegno chart (change the tens-row selection, keep the ones)
commonMisconceptions: Counting on in ones (56, 57, 58…66) instead of jumping a ten — no place-value shortcut.
Changing the ones digit as well, or changing the wrong digit (56 → 57 for '10 more').
Miscounting on the 100-square by moving diagonally or the wrong direction.
Struggling at decade boundaries because the pattern is memorised without understanding the tens digit's role.

learn.summary: For ages 6-7: mentally find 10 more or 10 less than a two-digit number without counting on in ones, by recognising that adding/subtracting a ten changes only the tens digit while the ones digit stays the same (10 more than 56 is 66; 10 less is 46). The core objective is reasoning plus fluency: the child should both produce the answer instantly and explain why only the tens digit changes. Concrete models (100-square vertical moves, base-ten rods) build the insight; timed recall practice consolidates it once understanding is secure. Keep examples within the two-digit range where only the tens digit changes by one.

activities.title: The 100-square vertical jump
feedback: If the child moves diagonally or sideways, point out that +10/-10 keeps the SAME column — only the row changes.

If the child moves in the wrong direction, link 'more' to the direction in which the numbers get bigger (down the grid on a top-down 100-square) and 'less' to the direction in which they get smaller (up).
Ask the child to compare the ones digit before and after: it should be identical every time.
When the child traces the vertical stripe, highlight that the move looks the same for every jump, which is why the shortcut always works.
activities.rationale: The 100-square's vertical structure makes 'ones unchanged, tens ±1' directly visible, so the child can see the pattern rather than memorise it. An optional interactive version — tap a number, press +10/-10, the highlight slides one row and the ones digit locks/glows while the tens digit ticks — may make the mechanism concrete, but a paper 100-square with a finger works for the move itself.
sourceClaims: The 100-square's vertical structure is a canonical model for ±10, making the unchanged ones digit visible.
Pupils are given a number and identify one more and one less, and develop mental place-value strategies including adding/subtracting tens.
learnerActions: Point to a starting number on a 100-square (for example 56).

On a 100-square numbered from the top (1-10 in the top row), to find 10 more, move straight DOWN exactly one row, staying in the same column; to find 10 less, move straight UP one row in the same column. (On a bottom-up 100-square the directions are reversed. Check which way the numbers grow on your grid.)
Say the new number aloud (56 → 66 for 10 more, 56 → 46 for 10 less).
Repeat the +10 jump several times to trace a straight vertical stripe down the grid: 56 → 66 → 76 → 86.
Each time, name the ones digit and the tens digit and state what changed: 'the ones stayed 6, the tens went up by one.'
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting ten is always the same move — straight down or up one row — and the ones digit never moves because only a whole ten is added or removed.

activities.title: Add or remove one ten-rod
feedback: If the child disturbs the cubes, reset and emphasise that only a rod is added or removed.
Ask: 'How many cubes before? How many after?' to confirm the ones are unchanged.
Connect back to the written number: the tens digit changed by one, the ones digit is identical.
activities.rationale: Physically adding/removing a single rod narrates the place-value reason the ones stay put, reinforcing the 100-square move with a different, hands-on representation. An optional screen toggle can grey out the ones-cubes to show they didn't move, but real rods give the same narrative through handling.
sourceClaims: Pupils are given a number and identify one more and one less, and develop mental place-value strategies including adding/subtracting tens.
learnerActions: Lay out a two-digit number with base-ten tens-rods and ones-cubes (for example 5 rods and 6 cubes for 56).
To add 10, place exactly ONE more rod; to subtract 10, take exactly ONE rod away.
Watch the ones-cubes the whole time and say aloud that they did not move.
Read the new total and state which digit changed (the tens) and which stayed the same (the ones).
activities.intendedInsight: Adding ten means adding a single ten-rod, which changes the tens count by one and leaves the ones completely untouched.

activities.title: Ten more versus one more
feedback: If the child answers '10 more than 56 is 57,' show that 57 is only ONE more — use the rods or 100-square to add a full ten and reach 66.
Reinforce: '1 more adds one cube; 10 more adds one rod.'
activities.rationale: A common error is confusing 10 more with 1 more or altering the wrong digit. Deliberately contrasting the two operations helps the child distinguish changing the ones from changing the tens.
sourceClaims: Pupils are given a number and identify one more and one less, and develop mental place-value strategies including adding/subtracting tens.
learnerActions: For the same starting number (for example 56), find 1 more and then 10 more; then find 1 less and 10 less.
Say which digit changes each time: 1 more changes the ones (56 → 57); 10 more changes the tens (56 → 66).
Explain in your own words how '10 more' is different from '1 more.'
activities.intendedInsight: Changing the ones digit (±1) and changing the tens digit (±10) are distinct moves; the child must adjust the correct digit for the correct operation.

activities.title: Mental fluency and explanation
feedback: If the child reaches the answer by counting (57, 58 … 66) with fingers or whispering, don't just reteach the answer — return to adding one ten-rod and show only the tens column changed, then rebuild toward saying it without counting.
If one direction (more) is reliable but the other (less) is not, practise the weaker direction with the 100-square move first.
Always ask the child to explain: 'Which digit changed? Why only that one?'

If the child meets a case like 10 more than 90, note it becomes 100 — a three-digit number where a hundreds digit appears, so it sits beyond the two-digit 'only the tens digit changes' pattern; treat it as a separate extension, not a routine check.
activities.rationale: This is a fluency skill, so timed/scored practice is appropriate once the concept is built. Watching the method (instant vs counting) is as important as the answer; requiring the explanation keeps it reasoning rather than rote. Formats such as fill-in-the-blank, multiple choice spotting the wrong-digit error, ordering a +10 sequence, or a ±10 slider on a 0-100 number line are all suitable.
sourceClaims: Given a two-digit number, mentally find 10 more or 10 less without counting, and explain the reasoning (1.NBT.5).
Pupils are given a number and identify one more and one less, and develop mental place-value strategies including adding/subtracting tens.
learnerActions: Answer rapid spoken or written items: 10 more than 73? (83) 10 less than 40? (30) 10 more than 56? (66) 10 less than 56? (46).
Give each answer without fingers or counting on in ones.
Complete a +10 chain by filling blanks: 46 → 56 → 66 → __ (76).
After answering, state which digit changed and why the ones digit did not.
Rehearse items that cross a decade boundary while the result stays a two-digit number (for example 10 more than 85 is 95, 10 less than 40 is 30) to check the pattern holds.
activities.intendedInsight: Once the place-value reason is understood, 10 more/10 less becomes instant recall produced by a single tens-digit change rather than by counting, for results that remain two-digit numbers.

constraints: Move from concrete models (100-square, rods) to the mental generalisation fairly quickly, and demand the explanation ('the ones stay the same, the tens go up/down by one'), not just the answer.

A static annotated 100-square is a useful reference for the pattern, but it does not let the child perform the jump and watch the ones hold still; use it alongside, not instead of, an activity where the child makes the move.

Scored/timed practice consolidates recall but assesses output; it is best used AFTER the place-value concept is built, and it does not on its own reveal whether the child is counting or jumping — watch the method during practice.
Multiple-choice/recognition items can spot wrong-digit errors but do not elicit independent construction of the answer or the explanation; include production items too.
Keep practice within the two-digit range where only the tens digit changes by one; 90→100 introduces a hundreds digit and is an extension case, not a routine item for this objective.
Rehearse decade crossings (e.g. 10 less than 40 = 30) deliberately, since a pattern memorised without understanding often breaks down there.
Distinguish '1 more / 1 less' explicitly from '10 more / 10 less'; confusing 10 more with 1 more is a common error.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the cited sources, the DfE National Curriculum claim was marked verified in the source row; the CCSS-M 1.NBT.5 claim and the NCETM 100-square claim were marked not verified. Treat the latter two as unconfirmed.

The legacy row framed open dialogue and 3D models as 'poor' and a picture as unable to let the child perform the jump. These are reasonable fit observations for this specific dynamic skill but have been softened to narrow affordances: a static image can still support the pattern as a reference, and conversation can be used to elicit the required explanation. They are not universal claims about medium superiority.

Arithmetic check: 10 more than 56 = 66, 10 less than 56 = 46, 10 more than 73 = 83, 10 less than 40 = 30, +10 chain 46→56→66→76 — all correct, all two-digit results where only the tens digit changes by one. The '10 more than 90' example is excluded from routine practice because 90+10=100 leaves the two-digit range and introduces a hundreds digit, so the 'only the tens digit changes by one' rule does not cleanly hold; it is retained only as an explicitly flagged extension case.
Independent re-audit confirms the two-digit scope fix is applied at every learner-facing occurrence (activity[3] actions, feedback, summary, and constraints).

probeDeeper: Which digit changed when you added 10? Why only that one?
10 more than 73 — did the ones digit change at all?
10 less than 40 — what happens to the ones digit?
assess.correctAnswer: 66, 46, 83, 30 — produced instantly by changing the tens digit by one, without counting on in ones.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts on or back in ones (fingers/whispering) instead of jumping a whole ten
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the answer — make the ten visible: add a tens rod on a base-ten mat and show only the tens column changed. Build toward saying it without counting.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child reaches 66 but by counting 57, 58 … 66; slow, with fingers.

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes the ones digit instead of the tens: '10 more than 56 is 57'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast 'one more' vs 'ten more' on a base-ten model; ten more adds a ten (tens digit +1), the ones stay put.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer differs from the given number by 1, not 10.

responseLevels.gap: Alters the wrong digit, or can only reach the answer by counting on in ones.
responseLevels.full: Instantly gives 10 more/less by adjusting the tens digit and explains the ones digit is unchanged.
responseLevels.partial: Gets answers by counting a ten in steps, or is reliable one direction (more) but not the other (less).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask quickly and watch how they get the answer (fingers? counting? or instant?): '10 more than 56? ... 10 less than 56? ... 10 more than 73? ... 10 less than 40?' Watch whether the tens digit jumps in one move.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The task is timed against counting: a child who understands 10-more as a single tens-jump answers immediately and can say only the tens digit changed; a child without it counts on ten ones (fingers, whispering) or alters the wrong digit. Watching the METHOD, not just the answer, is the point.
